questions.question_text: Which of the following options is recommended by NICE for the management of distress in patients with delirium?
questions.explanation:
Delirium (management) 
Pharmacological management of delirium 
 
Haloperidol has been shown to be of prophylactic use in delirium. 
 
NICE guidelines recommend short term haloperidol or olanzapine where delirium is associated with distress. 
 
Non-pharmacological management 
 
The following are recommended by NICE to assist in the management of delirium:- 
 Appropriate lighting and clear signage (use of calendars and a clock) 
 Talking to the person to reorientate them 
 Cognitively stimulating activities (e.g. reminiscence) 
 Regular visits from family and friends 
 Promote good sleep patterns

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most helpful in differentiating dementia from delirium?

options.text: Changes in the sleep wake cycle

questions.explanation:
Delirium and dementia differ in several ways but the main difference is the presence of fluctuating levels of consciousness. 
Delirium 
 
Delirium (aka 'acute confusional state') is characterised by an acute decline in both the level of consciousness and cognition with 
particular impairment in attention. Delirium often involves perceptual disturbances, abnormal psychomotor activity, and sleep-wake 
cycle impairment. 
 
Note: fluctuating consciousness is also known as clouding of consciousness and refers to a situation where the patient is out of 
touch with their environment and cannot respond properly to external stimuli such as conversation. 
 
Delirium typically comes on over a few days and has a fluctuating course.  
 
The causes of delirium are numerous and varied ranging from metabolic disturbances to medications. 
 
It is important to be able to differentiate delirium from dementia, the following table illustrates the main differences 
 
Delirium Dementia 
Onset brief gradual 
Disorientation occurs early occurs late 
Conciousness clouding occurs early normal until late stages 
Course fluctuates consistent 
Psychomotor change occurs early occurs late 
 
The clinical presentation can be classified broadly into three subtypes: 
 hypoactive 
 hyperactive 
 mixed 
 
Patients with hyperactive delirium demonstrate features of restlessness, agitation and hyper vigilance and often experience 
hallucinations and delusions. By contrast, patients with hypoactive delirium present with lethargy and sedation, respond slowly 
to questioning, and show little spontaneous movement. The hypoactive form occurs most frequently in elderly patients, and 
these patients are frequently overlooked or misdiagnosed as having depression or a form of dementia. Patients with mixed 
delirium demonstrate both hyperactive and hypoactive features

questions.question_text: Which of the following is recommended by NICE in the management of non-cognitive symptoms of dementia?
questions.explanation:
Dementia (non-cognitive symptoms) 
NICE recommend the following non pharmacological interventions for the management of non-cognitive symptoms in dementia:- 
 Aromatherapy 
 Multisensory stimulation 
 Therapeutic use of music and/or dancing 
 Animal-assisted therapy 
 Massage

questions.question_text: Syllogomania refers to which of the following?

options.text: Abnormal belief that one is divinely inspired
Abnormal tendency towards grand or grandiose behaviour

questions.explanation:
The suffix -mania indicates a compulsion or obsession. 
 
Pathological indecisiveness = aboulomania 
Abnormal tendency towards grand or grandiose behaviour = megalomania 
Abnormal belief that one is divinely inspired = entheomania 
Irrational predilection for stealing = kleptomania

questions.question_text: A 72 year old man develops a major depressive illness following a stroke. Whilst discussing treatment options he tells you that he had a gastric bleed 4 years ago. Which of the following would be the preferred treatment in this case?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2012 
 
In view of his previous GI bleed it would be sensible to avoid an SSRI given that they are known to increase the risk of subsequent 
bleeds. Nortriptyline is specifically recommended by the Maudsley Guidelines for post-stroke depression. 
 
The risk of GI bleeds from SSRIs appears to be linked to the reduced ability of platelets to form clots following serotonin uptake into 
the platelets. Theoretically, tricyclics could have a similar effect, however no effect has been seen (Walraven, 2001). Interestingly, 
the Maudsley Guidelines make no recommendation for patients who are at risk from GI bleeds who require antidepressants. 
Depression (post stroke) 
Post stroke depression is common (30-40%). Lesions in the vicinity of the left hemisphere basal ganglia tend to play a crucial role in 
the development of major depression after the acute stage of stroke (Herrmann 1995). 
 
Treatment needs to take into consideration any medical co-morbidity and other treatment (e.g. warfarin). 
 
The following drugs are recommended for post stroke depression:- 
 SSRIs 
 Mirtazapine 
 Nortriptyline 
 
Fluoxetine, citalopram, and nortriptyline are the most studied and seem to be effective and safe. 
 
If patients are on warfarin then citalopram or escitalopram is recommended. 
 
Prophylaxis 
 
In view of the high incidence of depression following stroke there has been considerable research into antidepressant prophylaxis. 
 
The following have been shown to be effective at preventing post stroke depression:- 
 Nortriptyline 
 Fluoxetine 
 Escitalopram 
 Sertraline 
 Mirtazapine 
 
Mianserin appears to be ineffective. 
 
Maudsley Guidelines 11th Edition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications is most likely to cause delirium?
questions.explanation:
Delirium (medication related) 
Delirium can sometimes arise as a consequence of medication use. The following list highlights some of the more common 
medications that can cause delirium:- 
 Anticholinergic drugs (tricyclic antidepressants) 
 Sedative hypnotics (benzodiazepines) 
 Corticosteroids 
 Anti-Parkinson drugs (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) 
 Histamine-2 (H2) blockers (cimetidine, ranitidine) 
 Centrally acting antihypertensives (methyldopa, reserpine) 
 Pain medication (opiates)

questions.question_text: A 70-year old woman whose sister was diagnosed with Alzheimer's wants to know the odds of her getting the disorder relevant to the normal population. Which of the following is the closest approximation of her increased risk?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2015 
Exam Question Mar 2011 
Alzheimer's (familial risk) 
The risk to the first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who develop the disorder at any time up to the age of 85 
years is increased some threefold to fourfold relative to the risk in controls.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding fronto-temporal lobar dementias?

options.text: They tend to have a late onset
Compared to Alzheimer's recent memory is preserved better than remote memory
They tend to have an acute onset
Lewy body dementia is a type of fronto-temporal lobar degeneration
Personality is preserved better than in Alzheimer's

correct_answer.text: Compared to Alzheimer's recent memory is preserved better than remote memory

questions.explanation:
Frontotemporal lobar degeneration 
Frontotemporal lobar degeneration is the third most common type of cortical dementia after Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia.  
 
There are three recognised types of FTLD 
 Frontotemporal dementia (Pick's) 
 Progressive non fluent aphasia (chronic progressive aphasia, CPA) 
 Semantic dementia 
 
Common features of frontotemporal lobar dementias 
Onset before 65 
Insidious onset 
Relatively preserved memory and visuospatial skills 
Personality change and social conduct problems 
 
Pick's 
 
This is the most common type and is characterised by personality change and impaired social conduct. Other common features 
include hyperorality, disinhibition, increased appetite, and perseveration behaviours. 
 
Focal gyral atrophy with a knife-blade appearance is characteristic of Pick's disease. The term kinfe-blade is used to describe the 
gyri that are thin and narrow and resemble knives. 
 
CPA 
 
Here the chief factor is non fluent speech. They make short utterances that are agrammatic. Comprehension is relatively preserved. 
 
Semantic dementia 
 
Here the patient has a fluent progressive aphasia. The speech is fluent but empty and conveys little meaning. Unlike in Alzheimer's 
memory is better for recent rather than remote events. 
 
Pathological changes seen in FTLD 
 
Macroscopic changes seen in Frontotemporal lobar degeneration include:- 
 Atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes 
 
Microscopic changes include:- 
 Pick bodies - spherical aggregations of tau protein 
 Gliosis 
 Neurofibrillary tangles 
 Senile plaques

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most appropriatly classified as a subcortical dementia?
questions.explanation:
Dementia (cortical versus sub-cortical) 
Attempts have been made to distinguish cortical dementia from subcortical dementia based on the clinical presentation. This is a 
contested area and many suggest the distinction is not possible. Nevertheless, questions on this appear in the exams. 
 
Cortical dementia is characterised by:-  
 Impaired memory 
 Impaired visuospatial ability 
 Impaired executive function 
 Impaired language 
 
Cortical dementias include:- 
 Alzheimer's disease 
 Pick's disease 
 Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease 
 
Subcortical dementia is characterised by:- 
 Generalised slowing of mental processes 
 Personality change 
 Mood disorders 
 Presence of abnormal movements 
 
Subcortical dementias include:-  
 Binswanger's disease 
 Dementia associated Huntington's disease 
 Dementia associated AIDS 
 Dementia associated with Parkinson's disease 
 Dementia associated with Wilson's disease 
 Dementia associated with progressive supranuclear palsy

questions.question_text: Of the following conditions, which one is not classified as frontotemporal lobar degeneration?
Which of the following is usually seen in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease?

options.text: Atrophy of the medial parietal lobe

questions.explanation:
Exam Question Sep 2011 
 
The earliest neuropathological changes occur in the medial temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus and parahippocampal 
gyrus. 
Alzheimer's (pathology) 
Macroscopic changes seen in Alzheimer's include:- 
 Hippocampal atrophy 
 Cerebral atrophy 
 Low brain weight 
 Enlargement of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle 
 
Microscopic changes seen in Alzheimer's include:- 
 Senile plaques (extracellular deposits of beta amyloid in the gray matter of the brain) 
 Neurofibrillary tangles (intracellular composition of tau protein) 
 Gliosis 
 Degeneration of the nucleus of Meynert 
 Hirano bodies 
 
These changes tend to occur in the cortex but also occur in the subcortical areas.  
 
Neurofibrillary tangles consist of hyperphosphorylated tau and plaques consist of a peptide called amyloid-beta, which is derived 
from amyloid precursor protein.

questions.question_text: A 70 year old lady is brought to A&E by her daughter who has noticed that her memory and personality have changed dramatically over the past 2-3 months. Prior to that she had been ok and was in relatively good health. Further questioning reveals fluctuating levels of consciousness. Which of the following would you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Any one of the options could account for the change in personality and cognition. However, the fluctuating levels of consciousness 
strongly suggest a chronic subdural haematoma. 
Dementia (differential diagnosis) 
Important differential diagnoses to consider in a person presenting with dementia include:- 
 delirium 
 depression

questions.question_text: Which of the following test would uncover a constructional apraxia?
questions.explanation:
Constructional apraxia is characterized by the inability to copy drawings or to manipulate objects to form patterns or designs. 
Clock drawing test 
The clock drawing test is used as a quick screening test for cognitive dysfunction. 
 
The patient is asked to draw a clock on a piece of paper, putting the numbers on the clock and drawing on the clock hands in the 
position of 10 minutes past 10. 
 
The test examines a range of different cognitive functions simultaneously, including:- 
 Visuospatial ability 
 Motor function 
 Attention 
 Comprehension

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a cortical rather than a subcortical dementia?
Which of the following is true regarding dementia due to Parkinson's disease? People with dementia due to Parkinson's tend to have greater problems with visual and verbal memory then

options.text: It is pathological distinct from dementia with Lewy bodies
Cognitive deficits such as alexia, dyspraxia, and anomia are less pronounced in dementia due to Parkinson's
Patients with new onset cognitive dysfunction are unlikely to have delirium
Drugs used in Parkinson's disease are not thought to affect cognitive function

correct_answer.text: Cognitive deficits such as alexia, dyspraxia, and anomia are less pronounced in dementia due to Parkinson's

questions.explanation:
dementia due to Parkinson's 
Dementia (with Parkinson's disease) 
Dementia is an acquired syndrome of decline in memory and at least one other cognitive domain (e.g. Language, visuospatial or 
executive dysfunction) that is sufficient to interfere with social and occupational function in an alert person. 
 
(American Psychiatric Association, 1994) 
Dementia due to Parkinson's disease 
 
Aside from the motor problems associated with Parkinson's disease are the non-motor symptoms including cognitive, behavioural, 
and psychological. 
 
Cognitive  
 
There is no clear agreement as to whether Lewy body dementia and dementia due to Parkinson's are pathologically different 
conditions. 
 
The drugs used to treat Parkinson's can interfere with cognitive function as can the neuroleptics. 
 
People with dementia due to Parkinson's disease tend to have marked problems with executive function. Verbal and visual memory 
are affected to a lesser extent. Other cognitive deficits, such as dysphasia, apraxia, alexia, agraphia, anomia and acalculia, are less 
pronounced. 
 
Cholinesterase inhibitors are useful in the treatment of cognitive problems associated with Parkinson's. They improve cognitive 
performance but are not well tolerated. A high proportion of patients develop side effects.

questions.question_text: When assessing a patient with the features of early dementia which of the following would suggest a sub- cortical rather than a cortical cause?
questions.explanation:
There is very little evidence to support this question. It is now accepted that the distinction between cortical and subcortical 
dementia is arbitrary. 
 
Having said this the college still use it as a question.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would suggest hypoactive delirium?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is facial inexpression, all the others would suggest hyperactive delirium. 
Delirium (hypo and hyperactive forms) 
Delirium can present in two different ways:- 
 Hyperactive delirium 
 Hypoactive delirium 
 
In hyperactive delirium the patient is generally aroused, hypervigilent, agitated, aggressive, and can experience hallucinations 
and/or delusions. Hypoactive delirium presents with decreased reactivity, motor and speech retardation, and facial inexpression. 
Hypoactive delirium is often missed and misdiagnosed as depression.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation:
During the 1960s and 1970s, aluminum emerged as a possible suspect in causing Alzheimer's disease. This suspicion led to 
concerns about everyday exposure to aluminum through sources such as cooking pots, foil, beverage cans, antacids and 
antiperspirants. Since then, studies have failed to confirm any role for aluminum in causing Alzheimer's. Almost all scientists today 
focus on other areas of research, and few experts believe that everyday sources of aluminum pose any threat. 
Alzheimer's (Risk factors) 
The following are recognised risk factors for the development of Alzheimer's disease:- 
 Age - Increasing age brings with it increased risks 
 Family history 
 Head trauma - especially if associated with loss of consciousness 
 Hypertension 
 Heart disease 
 Diabetes 
 CVA 
 High cholesterol 
 Lower educational level 
 Female gender

questions.question_text: A 70 year old man presents with a persistently low mood, early morning waking and a reduced appetite. His wife reports that he has stopped looking after himself but is still drinking adequate amounts of fluid; she thinks this is related to the death of the family dog. On further questioning the man reports odd beliefs and to hearing voices. Which of the following would you recommend in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
The mans presentation is consistent with psychotic depression. As the man is still eating and drinking ECT would not be 
appropriate at this stage but should be considered if other approaches fail. 
 
An antidepressant and antipsychotic would be the most appropriate treatment. Although the evidence does not clearly support this it 
is generally recommended as first line for psychotic depression. The choice between a TCA and SSRI is difficult as there are 
potential problems with both (GI bleeds, arrhythmias etc), on balance the TCA is preferable due to the fact that they are more 
effective. 
 
Maudsley Guidelines 11th Edition, p.234. 
Depression (psychotic) 
Surprisingly the evidence on treatments for psychotic depression is limited. The Maudsley Guidelines recommend the use of an 
antipsychotic in combination with an antidepressant as first line. The antidepressant should be a TCA rather than an SSRI.

questions.question_text: A patient with no significant psychiatric history develops an unexpected episode of mania at the age of 70. When you are admitting her it comes to your attention that she has recently been started on a number of new medications. Which of the following would be most likely to precipitate an episode of mania?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Mar 2011 
Mania (drug induced) 
There is good evidence that mania can be precipitated by the following:- 
 Levodopa 
 Corticosteroids 
 Anabolic-androgenic steroids 
 Antidepressants (tricyclic and monoamine oxidase inhibitor classes) 
 
There is also evidence (albeit weaker) that mania can be precipitated by:- 
 Dopaminergic anti-Parkinsonian drugs 
 Thyroxine 
 Iproniazid and isoniazid 
 Chloroquine

questions.question_text: Which of the following should be included in the basic investigation of dementia in all cases?
questions.explanation:
Dementia Investigation (NICE) 
NICE guidelines suggest the following investigations in people with dementia:- 
 routine haematology 
 biochemistry tests (including electrolytes, calcium, glucose, and renal and liver function) 
 thyroid function tests 
 serum vitamin B 12 and folate levels 
 Structural imaging should be used in the assessment of people with suspected dementia to exclude other cerebral 
pathologies and to help establish the subtype diagnosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred modality to 
assist with early diagnosis and detect subcortical vascular changes, although computed tomography (CT) scanning could 
be used. Imaging may not always be needed in those presenting with moderate to severe dementia, if the diagnosis is 
already clear. 
Perfusion hexamethylpropyleneamine oxime (HMPAO) single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) should be 
used to help differentiate Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia and frontotemporal dementia if the diagnosis is in doubt. 
People with Down's syndrome may show SPECT abnormalities throughout life that resemble those in Alzheimer's disease, 
so this test is not helpful in this group. 
 
If HMPAO SPECT is unavailable, 2-[18F]fluoro-2-deoxy-d-glucose positron emission tomography (FDGPET) should be 
considered to help differentiate between Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia and frontotemporal dementia if the 
diagnosis is in doubt. 
 
Dopaminergic iodine-123-radiolabelled 2-carbomethoxy-3-(4-iodophenyl)-N-(3-fluoropropyl) nortropane (FP-CIT) SPECT 
should be used to help establish the diagnosis in those with suspected dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) if the diagnosis is 
in doubt. 
 
Testing for syphilis serology or HIV should not be routinely undertaken in the investigation of people with suspected 
dementia. These tests should be considered only in those with histories suggesting they are at risk or if the clinical picture 
dictates. 
 
A midstream urine test should always be carried out if delirium is a possibility 
 
Clinical presentation should determine whether investigations such as chest X-ray or electrocardiogram are needed. 
 
Cerebrospinal fluid examination should not be performed as a routine investigation for dementia. Cerebrospinal fluid 
examination should be used if CreutzfeldtJakob disease or other forms of rapidly progressive dementia are suspected. 
 
Electroencephalography should not be used as a routine investigation in people with dementia. Electroencephalography 
should be considered if a diagnosis of delirium, frontotemporal dementia or CreutzfeldtJakob disease is suspected, or in 
the assessment of associated seizure disorder in those with dementia. 
 
Brain biopsy for diagnostic purposes should be considered only in highly selected people whose dementia is thought to be 
due to a potentially reversible condition that cannot be diagnosed in any other way

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a recognised risk factor for delirium?
questions.explanation:
Delirium (risk factors) 
Risk factors for delirium include:- 
 Age 65 years or older 
 Cognitive impairment (e.g. dementia) 
 Coexistent severe medical illness (e.g. infection)

questions.question_text: Regarding depression in the elderly, which of the following is true?

options.text: Fluoxetine should be used as first-line in depression in the elderly
Response to antidepressants is reduced in patients with a physical illness
Mirtazapine should be used as first-line in depression in the elderly
People aged over 65 should continue antidepressant therapy for at least 1 year following remission
Outcome following antidepressant therapy in the elderly is generally suboptimal

correct_answer.text: Outcome following antidepressant therapy in the elderly is generally suboptimal

questions.explanation:
Antidepressants (in the elderly) 
Summary of Maudsley Guidelines 
 
There is no ideal antidepressant recommended for elderly patients. Each group of antidepressants comes with its own problems. 
SSRIs are generally better tolerated than TCA but do carry a risk of GI bleeds and hyponatremia. Ultimately the choice of 
antidepressant is governed by the individual patient. 
 
The elderly tend to take longer to respond to antidepressants than younger patients. It is recommended that elderly patients 
continue taking antidepressants for at least 2 years following remission due to a high relapse rate in this time period (up to 60%). 
 
There is no evidence to suggest response to antidepressants is suboptimal in the physically ill. Outcome in the elderly is however 
generally suboptimal.  
 
Summary from Advances in Psychiatric Treatment article 2013 
 
First-line options 
 
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most common first-line treatment for late life depression. 
 
Sertraline has the best evidence for efficacy and tolerability, although there is also good evidence for escitalopram and citalopram in 
those over 65. All three have the advantage of a favorable side-effect profile and can be taken by people with a history of cognitive 
impairment and stroke. 
 
Although citalopram was previously recommended for use in those with cardiovascular disease, recent data have highlighted the 
risk of prolonged QT interval with the drug, and the maximum recommended dose for older adults has now been reduced. 
 
Citalopram should not be prescribed in conjunction with other agents that prolong the QT interval, such as antipsychotics and 
certain antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin). 
 
It is not yet clear whether the effect on the QT interval is specific to citalopram, or whether it represents a side-effect across SSRIs 
more generally. Until more data are obtained to support or refute this, sertraline could be considered the best first-line SSRI option 
for the treatment of late-life depression on the basis of efficacy and tolerability. 
 
Where SSRIs are contraindicated, or poorly tolerated, other classes of antidepressant can be used as first-line treatment. 
Mirtazapine is one alternative for first-line treatment in older adults. It has few cardiac side-effects and a weaker association with 
hyponatraemia. 
 
Tricyclic antidepressants should be used with caution because of the risk of cardiac side-effects (e.g. prolongation of QT interval 
with amitriptyline) and toxicity in overdose, and because their antimuscarinic effects are more likely to exacerbate cognitive 
impairment. 
 
Dosulepin and reboxetine are not recommended for use in older adults. 
 
Second-line options 
 
Venlafaxine has been proposed as a useful second-line antidepressant. It may exacerbate hypertension and therefore close 
monitoring of this is needed at treatment initiation. 
 
Combination and augmentation therapy 
 
Combining an SSRI with venlafaxine provides more effective treatment compared with augmentation by psychological therapy. 
Combining mirtazapine with venlafaxine may be associated with increased side-effects, without significant therapeutic benefit. 
Lithium can be used as an effective augmenting agent. Sodium valproate is not recommended as an augmenting agent in older 
adults. 
 
In cognitive impairment 
 
One randomised double-blind trial compared antidepressant plus donepezil with antidepressant plus placebo in patients with late-
life depression. The addition of donepezil resulted in no clear benefit in either preventing recurrence of depression or preventing the 
development of mild cognitive impairment or dementia. 
 
Maudsley Guidelines 12th Edition

questions.question_text: An elderly patient with a long history of mental health problems who is on a number of different medications attends clinic. They complain of poor physical health over the past six months. They have been experiencing constipation, lethargy, and have felt more depressed than normal. They also tell you that two weeks ago they were admitted to hospital and diagnosed with kidney stones. Which of the following of their prescribed medications would be the most likely cause for their symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Lithium is a recognised cause of hyperparathyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism refers to over action of parathyroid hormone which 
causes raised calcium. Symptoms of hypercalcemia include:- 
 Groans (constipation) 
 Stones (kidney stones) 
 Bones (bone pain) 
 Psychic moans (depression, lethargy, confusion) 
Lithium (side-effects) 
Side-effects of lithium include:- 
 Drowsiness 
 Dry mouth 
 Polyuria 
 Polydipsia 
 Nausea 
 Weight gain 
 Fine tremor 
 Metallic taste 
 Diarrhoea 
 Muscle weakness 
 
Side-effects are dose (plasma level) related. Propranolol can be helpful for fine tremor. Lithium is also known to exacerbate certain 
skin conditions including psoriasis and acne. 
 
Long-term use is associated with the following:- 
 Hypothyroidism 
 Irreversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus 
 Reduced GFR (chronic kidney disease) 
 Hyperparathyroidism

questions.question_text: An elderly male patient complained of a specific disturbance in memory that occurred whilst having sex. This episode lasted 6 hours and he was fully conscious throughout. He made a full recovery following the event. Select the most likely diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Transient global amnesia 
Transient global amnesia refers to a condition characterised by transient loss of memory. It typically affects those over 50 and 
spontaneously resolves within 24 hours. No clear cause has been identified but it has been proposed to be a variant of migraine, a 
form of epilepsy, and a presentation of a TIA (transient ischemic attack). 
 
Precipitants often include exertion, cold, pain, emotional stress, and sexual intercourse. 
 
Neurological examination at the time fails to demonstrate any other pathology other than memory impairment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding psychosis in Parkinson's disease? Neuroleptics can worsen movement disorders in Parkinson's disease

options.text: Hallucinations in dementia due to Parkinson's disease are less common than in Parkinsonâs disease without
Hallucinations involving landscapes are often reported
Antiparkinsonian drugs are used to treat psychotic symptoms
Neuroleptics can worsen movement disorders in Parkinson's disease

correct_answer.text: Neuroleptics can worsen movement disorders in Parkinson's disease

questions.explanation:
Exam Question Mar 2011 
Psychosis - associated with Parkinson's 
Psychiatric symptoms are common in Parkinson's disease and range from mild to severe. Factors associated with severe 
symptoms include age, sleep disturbance, dementia, and disease severity. 
 
Hallucinations are common in Parkinson's disease. They tend to be visual but can be auditory or tactile. These hallucinations 
commonly involve people or animals. Delusions are less common. 
 
In the majority of patients, psychotic symptoms are thought to be secondary to dopaminergic medication rather than due to the 
Parkinson's disease itself. However, hallucinations may occur independently of dopaminergic medication, based on reports of visual 
hallucinations in the pre-dopa era, which suggests that dopaminergic medication is not the direct cause of visual hallucinations, but 
seems to serve as a precipitating factor. 
 
Anticholinergics and dopamine agonists seem to be associated with a higher risk of inducing psychosis than levodopa or catechol-
O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitors. 
 
Medications used for psychotic symptoms may worsen movement problems. Risperidone and the atypicals should be avoided 
completely. Low dose quetiapine is the best tolerated. Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic drug for treating psychosis in 
Parkinson's disease but its use in clinical practice is limited by to need for monitoring and the additional physical risks. 
 
Cholinesterase inhibitors have been used to treat psychosis associated with dementia due to Parkinson's. There is very little data 
on this. Some results have shown them to be of benefit. 
 
Maudsley Guidelines 12th Edition

questions.question_text: A 71 year old male recently started on a new treatment has suddenly started texting his wife rude text messages and binge eating. Which of the following treatment would you suspect he has been started on?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Apr 2012 
Dopamine agonists 
Dopamine receptor agonists have a direct action on dopamine receptors. They are often used in the treatment of Parkinson's 
disease. Examples include:- 
 apomorphine 
 ropinirole 
 
These drugs are associated with psychiatric side effects (BNF 2012), particularly impulse control disorders such as:- 
 pathological gambling 
 binge eating 
 hypersexuality

questions.question_text: A 68-year old man with a history of depression has recently developed Parkinson's. His wife complains that in the last 2 weeks he has been sending her sexually-explicit messages, and accusing her of having an affair. What is the most likely drug to have caused this?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2010 
 
Ropinirole is a dopamine agonist used in the treatment of Parkinson's. Side effects include pathological gambling and hyperse xuality. 
Parkinson's disease 
Parkinson's disease is a degenerative disease of the brain. It is characterised by movement problems such as rigidity, bradykinesia (slowing of 
movement), and tremor.  
 
The principle abnormality is the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. There is an accumulation of 
alpha synuclein in these abnormal dopaminergic cells. These abnormal protein accumulations are referred to as Lewy bodies.  
 
The majority of cases of Parkinson are idiopathic (cause unknown).  
 
The tremor associated with Parkinson's disease is classically described a s 'pill rolling' due to the characteristic appearance of the fingers.  
 
Type of tremor Frequency 
Intention 2-3Hz 
Type of tremor Frequency 
Parkinsonian 5Hz 
Essential 7Hz 
Physiological 10Hz 
Psychogenic variable

A full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and bone profile are requested. Which other blood tests is it most appropriate to request?

questions.question_text: A patient is referred by their GP with memory problems. You establish a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment. Which of the following is recommended for prevention of dementia?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Jun 2008 
Mild cognitive impairment 
The term 'mild cognitive impairment' MCI is generally u sed to refer to a transitional zone between normal cognitive function and clinically probable 
Alzheimer's disease (AD). 
 
It represents a clinical syndrome that can be utilized to classify persons who do not fulfil a diagnosis of dementia, but who  have a high risk of 
progressing to a dementia disorder.  
 
General criteria for MCI:- 
 Not normal, not demented (Does not meet criteria (DSM IV, ICD 10) for a dementia syndrome)  
 Self and/or informant report and impairment on objective cognitive tasks  
 Evidence of decline over time on objective cognitive tasks and / or  
 Preserved basic activities of daily living / minimal impairment in complex instrumental functions  
 
When persons with MCI are followed over time, some progress to AD and other dementia types, but some are s table or even recover. 
 
The principal cognitive impairment can be amnestic, single nonmemory domain or involving multiple cognitive domains.  
 
There is also evidence that deficits in regional cerebral blood flow as measured by SPECT and regional cerebral gl ucose metabolism as measured 
by FDG-PET could predict future development of AD in individuals with MCI.  
 
There is no evidence for long-term efficacy of currently approved pharmacological treatments in MCI. Epidemiological studies have indicated a 
reduced risk of dementia in persons taking antihypertensive medications, cholesterol - lowering drugs, antioxidants, anti -inflammatories and 
oestrogen therapy; however, data from randomized clinical trials are needed to verify these associations.  
 
There are two clinical screening instruments which allow for a broad assessment of mild cognitive impairment —the CAMCog (part of the 
CAMDEX)20 and the SISCO (part of the SIDAM).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false regarding pharmacokinetics in the elderly?

options.text: The rate of absorption is slows with age
The volume of distribution for lipid-soluble drugs decreases with age
The elderly experience reduced hepatic blood flow which results in decreased metabolism
The absorption of drugs is less compared to younger adults
Advancing age is accompanied by decreased gastric motility

correct_answer.text: The volume of distribution for lipid-soluble drugs decreases with age

questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2010 
 
The elderly have decreased lean body mass, increased body fat, and decreased total body water. For this reason lipid soluble drugs show an 
increased volume of distribution with advanced age.  
Prescribing in the elderly 
Older people's bodies are different to those of younger adults and this affects how they handle medication. Additionally they  are often on a range of 
other drugs so interactions are an issue. 
 
Both pharmacokinetics and pharmcodynamic differences apply.  
 
Pharmacokinetics  
 
Changes in distribution, metabolism, and excretion are important.  
 
Absorption  
 
In old age there is reduced gastric acid secretion. This is accompan ied by decreased gastric motility, and reduced surface area available for 
absorption. Pharmacokinetic studies on the effect of ageing on drug absorption have provided conflicting results. While some studies have not 
shown significant age-related differences in absorption rates for different drugs, the absorption of vitamin B12, iron and calcium through active 
transport mechanisms is reduced, whereas the absorption of levodopa is increased.  
 
Distribution 
 
There is a relative reduction of body water to body f at (the elderly have more fat and less water) as the body ages which results in an altered 
distribution of lipid soluble drugs. Older people also have less albumin. These changes result in increased blood levels for water soluble drugs, 
decreased levels for lipid soluble drugs (increased volume of distribution), and a greater unbound free fraction (increased amount of active dru g). As 
people age, the half-life of a lipid soluble drug increases.  
 
Metabolism 
 
Hepatic metabolism of drugs decreases with age as a consequence of reduced hepatic blood flow and reduced enzyme activity.  
 
Excretion 
 
The kidneys become less effective with age (by 65, 35% of renal function is lost, and by 80, 50% is lost). Serum creatinine a nd urea is often used to 
estimate renal function but can be misleading in the elderly as they have less muscle and so produce less creatinine.   
 
The e-GFR is a tool that can be used to estimate renal function in the elderly.  
 
Drugs that are primarily excreted by the kidneys (e.g. lithium and sulpiride ) will tend to accumulate in the elderly and so small doses may be needed.  
 
Pharmcodynamics  
 
Receptor sensitivity tends to increase during old age and so this group tends to require smaller doses. It is generally recom mended that you start 
with half of the usual adult dose and go on from there. This increase in sensitivity contributes to an increased incidence of side -effects in the elderly. 
 
Older people tend to take longer to respond to treatment (the therapeutic response is delayed).

options.text: Bereavement has been shown to be a significant contributory factor for very late onset schizophrenia
Rates of depression in the elderly are significantly higher than in younger adults
The highest rates of suicide in the general population occur in elderly men
There is a trend towards lower rates of personality disorder with increasing age
A positive family history is the strongest risk factor for dementia

correct_answer.text: There is a trend towards lower rates of personality disorder with increasing age

questions.explanation:
Epidemiology of mental disorders among the elderly 
Depression 
 
Surprisingly, surveys of the elderly in the general population have recurrently found rates  of depression that are significantly lower than in younger 
adults. 
 
The prevalence of depressive symptoms is considerably higher in elderly persons consulting their doctor than in the general c ommunity. One study 
in London found a point prevalence of abou t 30 per cent (this is likely to be higher as GPs miss up to a third of mild cases).  
 
Suicide 
 
For many decades across the world, the traditional pattern has been for the highest rates of suicide to be in elderly men. Th is has now changed. 
 
In the United Kingdom in 2002, men aged 75 and over had a rate of 10 per 100 000, whereas the highest rate was 18 per 100 000, in men aged 3 5-
44 years. 
 
The main risk factors for suicide in the elderly include: 
 Past history of an attempt 
 Depressive disorder 
 Access to lethal means 
 Physical illness or disability 
 Chronic pain 
 Recent losses 
 Social isolation 
 
A systematic review of suicide prevention strategies for all age groups concluded that two interventions did reduce rates:   
 Physician education in recognising and treating depression 
 Restricting access to lethal means.  
 
Personality disorder 
 
There is limited information on the prevalence of personality disorders in the general population. That said, there is a tren d towards lower rates with 
increasing age. 
 
Psychosis 
 
Psychosis with onset after the age of 60 years (very late -onset schizophrenia) has a 1-year prevalence of of 0.1 to 0.5 per cent. It is more common 
in women. 
 
An association has been found with sensory impairment (deafness or poor eyesight). Personal an d environmental factors associated with ageing 
have been considered, such as physical ill health, bereavement, loss of friends, and loss of income, but these have not been   
shown to contribute significantly.  
 
Genetic factors appear to be less important tha n in earlier onset schizophrenia.  
 
Alcohol misuse 
 
Precise figures and prevalence rates are unreliable. The standard (and widely used) assessment tools are probably not valid i n this group. 
 
Studies in the elderly consistently find that men have higher rat es of alcohol misuse than women.  
 
Dementia 
 
Dementia incidence is similar in all continents and from different regions of the world. Alzheimer's accounts for 60 -70 per cent and vascular 
dementia accounts for 15-20 per cent  
of all dementia cases. 
 
Age is the strongest risk factor for dementia. Approximately 48% of people aged 95 and over have dementia.

questions.question_text: An elderly man admitted to a medical ward is noted to be confused and experiencing agitation. He has a cardiac pacemaker. What investigation would you do to assist in the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2012 
 
The mans case suggests he is delirious and one would want to perform some structural imaging to rule out intracranial pathology 
such as a subdural. That narrows the above choice to either MRI or CT. Traditionally a cardiac pacemaker has been a 
contraindication to having an MRI, making a CT the preferred option here. 
 
Note however that some MRI scanners can now run protocols meaning that patients with cardiac pacemakers can be safely 
scanned. Most scanners will not be able to do this currently however. 
Neuroimaging techniques 
Traditionally Neuroimaging has been divided into structural and functional types. This is becoming increasingly difficult to do as 
techniques develop that cover both aspects. 
 
Structural 
 
Computed Tomography (CT) - CT uses ionising x-ray radiation. A beam of x-ray's which is directed through the head rotates around 
to produce a 2-D picture. Dense tissues such as bone attenuate (reduce in intensity) x-rays the most and appear white, whereas 
tissues such as air attenuate the least and appear black. 
 
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capitalises on the inherent magnetic properties of tissues. First a large magnetic field is applied 
that aligns all the hydrogen atoms in the same direction. Then a radio frequency is applied that realigns the atoms (Larmour 
frequency). Once the radio frequency is turned off the atoms realign and give of a signal in the process. This signal is detected by 
the MRI machine to produce an image. T1 and T2 weighting refers to the way atoms realign after the radio frequency is removed. 
 
Functional 
 
Functional MRI (fMRI) takes advantage of the fact that blood with different levels of oxygenation produces different signals. It 
therefore is a measure of oxygen consumption. This technique is called blood level-dependent (BOLD) contrast. 
 
Emission tomography (PET and SPECT) - Both positron emission tomography (PET) and single photon emission computer 
tomography (SPECT) involve detecting emissions from radioactive substances that have been injected. SPECT detects gamma 
rays as substance decays whereas PET detects them following collisions of poistrons and electrons. PET is more expensive but 
offers better spatial and temporal resolution. Several nucleotides are used in PET including N13 (nitrogen), C11, O15, F18. F18 is 
used most widely. 
 
Perfusion MRI (pMRI) - This technique evaluates microscopic blood flow in capillaries. 
 
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) - This allows chemical sampling of the brain. It does not produce an image instead it 
gives a breakdown of the amounts of different chemicals that are in an area of the brain. It can be used to look at specific 
metabolites such as glutamate. 
 
Combined (both structural and functional) 
 
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) - DTI provides a method for estimating the paths water takes as it diffuses through white matter, and 
so showing white matter tracts. It is a form of MRI.

International epidemiological findings 
 
Dementia is largely a disease of older people, but 2% of those affected are under 65 years of age. 
 
The most recent meta-analysis of European population-based studies carried out in the 1990s, the EURODEM study, used data 
from 11 studies carried out in eight European countries. There were no important differences in the age-specific prevalence 
between studies or between countries. The overall prevalence for males and females doubles for every five year increase in age

average disease duration (from onset to death) of four years. Clinical studies have suggested a duration of 5-7 years from

questions.question_text: A 74 year old man who has been taking sertraline for a depressive illness along with CBT is now in remission. He is happy with his treatment and apart from an occasional dry mouth does not suffer any side effects from his medication. How long should he continue taking sertraline?

options.text: As he is having CBT he can stop sertraline as soon as he achieves remission

questions.explanation:
People over 65 should continue antidepressant medication for at least 2 years following remission, this regardless of any 
psychological therapy that they are using. 
Antidepressants (in the elderly) 
Summary of Maudsley Guidelines 
 
There is no ideal antidepressant recommended for elderly patients. Each group of antidepressants comes with its own problems. 
SSRIs are generally better tolerated than TCA but do carry a risk of GI bleeds and hyponatremia. Ultimately the choice of 
antidepressant is governed by the individual patient. 
 
The elderly tend to take longer to respond to antidepressants than younger patients. It is recommended that elderly patients 
continue taking antidepressants for at least 2 years following remission due to a high relapse rate in this time period (up to 60%). 
 
There is no evidence to suggest response to antidepressants is suboptimal in the physically ill. Outcome in the elderly is however 
generally suboptimal.  
 
Summary from Advances in Psychiatric Treatment article 2013 
 
First-line options 
 
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most common first-line treatment for late life depression. 
 
Sertraline has the best evidence for efficacy and tolerability, although there is also good evidence for escitalopram and citalopram in 
those over 65. All three have the advantage of a favorable side-effect profile and can be taken by people with a history of cognitive 
impairment and stroke. 
 
Although citalopram was previously recommended for use in those with cardiovascular disease, recent data have highlighted the 
risk of prolonged QT interval with the drug, and the maximum recommended dose for older adults has now been reduced. 
 
Citalopram should not be prescribed in conjunction with other agents that prolong the QT interval, such as antipsychotics and 
certain antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin). 
 
It is not yet clear whether the effect on the QT interval is specific to citalopram, or whether it represents a side-effect across SSRIs 
more generally. Until more data are obtained to support or refute this, sertraline could be considered the best first-line SSRI option 
for the treatment of late-life depression on the basis of efficacy and tolerability. 
 
Where SSRIs are contraindicated, or poorly tolerated, other classes of antidepressant can be used as first-line treatment. 
Mirtazapine is one alternative for first-line treatment in older adults. It has few cardiac side-effects and a weaker association with 
hyponatraemia. 
 
Tricyclic antidepressants should be used with caution because of the risk of cardiac side-effects (e.g. prolongation of QT interval 
with amitriptyline) and toxicity in overdose, and because their antimuscarinic effects are more likely to exacerbate cognitive 
impairment. 
 
Dosulepin and reboxetine are not recommended for use in older adults. 
 
Second-line options 
 
Venlafaxine has been proposed as a useful second-line antidepressant. It may exacerbate hypertension and therefore close 
monitoring of this is needed at treatment initiation. 
 
Combination and augmentation therapy 
 
Combining an SSRI with venlafaxine provides more effective treatment compared with augmentation by psychological therapy. 
Combining mirtazapine with venlafaxine may be associated with increased side-effects, without significant therapeutic benefit. 
Lithium can be used as an effective augmenting agent. Sodium valproate is not recommended as an augmenting agent in older 
adults. 
 
In cognitive impairment 
 
One randomised double-blind trial compared antidepressant plus donepezil with antidepressant plus placebo in patients with late-
life depression. The addition of donepezil resulted in no clear benefit in either preventing recurrence of depression or preventing the 
development of mild cognitive impairment or dementia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a licensed treatment for insomnia?
questions.explanation:
Promethazine is licensed for short term sedation, allergy and urticaria, and nausea and vomiting. It is NOT licensed for insomnia. 
Insomnia (treatments) 
The NICE (2015) Clinical Knowledge Summary provides a useful guide on the management of insomnia. It splits the management 
into that of short-term insomnia (<4 weeks) and long-term insomnia (>4 weeks). 
 
Short-term insomnia: 
 
Consider a short course of a hypnotic drug only if daytime impairment is severe. 
 
The hypnotics recommended for the treatment of insomnia are: 
 Short-acting benzodiazepines temazepam, loprazolam, lormetazepam. 
 Non-benzodiazepines (the 'z-drugs') zopiclone, zolpidem, and zaleplon (all are short acting). 
 Diazepam is not generally recommended, but it can be useful if insomnia is associated with daytime anxiety 
 
If a hypnotic is prescribed: 
 Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period possible. The exact duration will depend on the underlying cause, but 
treatment should not continue for longer than 2 weeks. 
 Inform the person that further prescriptions for hypnotics will not usually be given, ensure that the reasons for this are 
understood, and document this in the person's notes. 
 Do not issue further prescriptions without seeing the person again. 
 If there has been no response to the first hypnotic, do not prescribe another. 
 If the person experiences adverse effects considered to be directly related to an hypnotic, consider switching to another 
hypnotic. 
 
Long-term insomnia 
 
Refer to psychological services for a cognitive or behavioural intervention. 
 
Pharmacological therapy is generally not recommended for the long-term management of insomnia but may be considered for 
immediate relief of symptoms. 
 
If prescribing medication, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period possible. The exact duration will depend on the 
underlying cause but should not continue for longer than 2 weeks. Up to 4 weeks' use may occasionally be required, but continued 
use should always be re-assessed after 2 weeks. 
 
For people over 55 years of age with persistent insomnia, consider treatment with a modified-release melatonin. The recommended 
initial duration of treatment is 3 weeks. If there is a response to treatment, it can be continued for a further 10 weeks. 
 
Additional detail from NICE regarding evidence base: 
 
There is insufficient evidence to assess the effectiveness of sleep hygiene as a single intervention; however its use is widely 
supported by expert opinion in current literature and guidelines.  
 
There is good evidence for the efficacy of hypnotic drugs in short-term insomnia; however, their use is associated with adverse 
effects. 
 
Tolerance to the hypnotic effects of benzodiazepine may be rapid, and may occur within a few days or weeks of regular use. 
 
Dependence is more likely to develop with long-term use, high doses, more potent or shorter-acting benzodiazepines, and a history 
of anxiety problems.  
 
Diazepam, nitrazepam, and flurazepam are not recommended because their long half-life commonly gives rise to next-day residual 
effects, and repeated doses tend to be cumulative. 
 
Sedative drugs other than hypnotics (such as antidepressants, antihistamines, choral hydrate, clomethiazole, and barbiturates) are 
not recommended for the management of insomnia. Expert opinion from reviews suggests that there is insufficient evidence to 
support their use, and that the potential for adverse effects is significant. 
 
Modified-release melatonin (Circadin®) is only licensed for the management of primary insomnia (usually defined as more than 4 
weeks' duration), and has only been studied in people with long-term insomnia. 
 
The evidence on the efficacy of acupuncture is generally of poor methodological quality with inconsistent results. There is some 
evidence from single studies in a Cochrane systematic review to suggest that acupuncture and its variants (acupressure and 
transcutaneous electrical stimulation) may improve quality of sleep. Results for other sleep variables were inconsistent. 
 
There is insufficient good quality evidence to make a recommendation regarding the efficacy of valerian, or any other herbal 
remedies, in the management of insomnia. 
 
Good sleep hygiene includes: 
 Establish fixed times for going to bed and waking up (and avoid sleeping in after a poor night's sleep). 
 Try to relax before going to bed. 
 Maintain a comfortable sleeping environment: not too hot, cold, noisy, or bright. 
 Avoid napping during the day. 
 Avoid caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol within 6 hours of going to bed. (Consider complete elimination of caffeine from the 
diet.) 
 Avoid exercise within 4 hours of bedtime (although exercise earlier in the day is beneficial). 
 Avoid eating a heavy meal late at night. 
 Avoid watching or checking the clock throughout the night. 
 Only use the bedroom for sleep and sexual activity.

questions.question_text: A 65 year old man is referred by his general practitioner due to a concern about cognitive impairment confirmed by a score of 19 on the MMSE. His CT scan shows atrophy and white matter hyperintensities. Which of the following would constitute the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2013 
 
This is a common CT result from a patient with Alzheimer's dementia. Differentiating Alzheimer's from vascular dementia is very 
difficult even with the help of imaging. There is some evidence that donepazil is effective in vascular dementia. There is no 
evidence to support the use of aspirin in vascular dementia as confirmed by a previous Cochrane review (Rands 2000). 
 
Rands (2000) Aspirin for vascular dementia. The Cochrane library 23 Oct 2000. 
Alzheimer's (treatment) 
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (AChE inhibitors) prevent cholinesterase from breaking down acetylcholine. Acetylcholine is deficient 
in Alzheimer's and therefore they are useful in this condition. 
 
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors used in the management of Alzheimer's include:- 
 Donepezil (specific and reversible inhibitor of AChE) 
 Galantamine (selective, competitive and reversible inhibitor of AChE, also enhances the effect of acetylcholine on nicotinic 
receptors) 
 Rivastigmine (an AChE and butyrylcholinesterase inhibitor) 
 
Gastrointestinal side effects from these drugs (nausea and vomiting) are common. 
 
In addition to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors a drug called memantine is also used. This is an NMDA receptor antagonist that blocks 
the effects of pathologically elevated levels of glutamate that may lead to neuronal dysfunction. 
 
NICE make the following recommendations about the treatment of Alzheimer's disease:- 
 The three acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are recommended as options for 
managing mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease 
 Memantine is recommended as an option for managing Alzheimer's disease for people with moderate Alzheimer's disease 
who are intolerant of or have a contraindication to AChE inhibitors or for severe Alzheimer's disease 
 
Where severity is defined as follows:- 
 Mild = MMSE 21-26 
 Moderate = MMSE 10-20 
 Severe = MMSE 0-10 
 
Side effects of the antidementia drugs include cholinergic effects such as nausea, diarrhea, and dizziness.

questions.question_text: An acquired syndrome of decline in memory and at least one other cognitive domain (e.g. Language, visuospatial, or executive dysfunction) sufficient to interfere with social an occupational function in an alert person' describes which of the following conditions?
Complex visual hallucinations occurring in clear consciousness which is associated with visual impairment is most indicative of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Todd syndrome is another term for Alice in Wonderland syndrome which is a neurological condition in which a patient's sense of 
body image, space, and/or time are distorted. Sufferers may experience micropsia or Lilliputian hallucinations, macropsia, or other 
sensorial distortions, including altered sense of velocity. 
 
Diogenes syndrome is a condition characterized by extreme self-neglect, social withdrawal, lack of shame, apathy, and compulsive 
hoarding of rubbish. It is found mainly in the elderly and is associated with progressive dementia. 
Charles Bonnet syndrome 
Charles Bonnet syndrome 
 
Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS) is characterised by persistent or recurrent complex hallucinations (usually visual or auditory), 
occurring in clear consciousness. This is generally against a background of visual impairment (although visual impairment is not 
mandatory for a diagnosis). Insight is usually preserved. This must occur in the absence of any other significant neuropsychiatric 
disturbance. 
 
Risk factors include: 
 Advanced age 
 Peripheral visual impairment 
 Social isolation 
 Sensory deprivation 
 Early cognitive impairment 
 
CBS is equally distributed between sexes and does not show any familial predisposition. The most common opthalmological 
conditions associated with this syndrome are age-related macular degeneration, followed by glaucoma and cataract. 
 
Well-formed complex visual hallucinations are thought to occur in 10-30 percent of individuals with severe visual impairment. 
Prevalence of CBS in visually impaired people is thought to be between 11 and 15 percent. 
 
Around a third find the hallucinations themselves an unpleasant or disturbing experience. In a large study published in the British 
Journal of Ophthalmology, 88% had CBS for 2 years or more, resolving in only 25% at 9 years (thus it is not generally a transient 
experience).

questions.question_text: A 78 year old woman with heart disease has recently been started on fluoxetine for a moderate depressive illness. She visits her GP complaining of tiredness and muscle cramps. The GP contacts you for advice, which of the following is most likely to reveal an abnormality?
questions.explanation:
The womans history is most consistent with a diagnosis of SIADH caused by the antidepressant she has started using, this would 
manifest in the U & E which would show a low sodium level. 
Hyponatremia 
Hyponatremia (low serum sodium) in psychiatric patients may result from the psychiatric disorder itself, from its treatment, or from 
concomitant medical conditions. 
 
Symptoms include:- 
 Nausea and vomiting 
 Confusion and lethargy 
 Irritability 
 Muscular spasm and cramp 
 Seizures 
 
Where hyponatremia is drug induced it is referred to as 'the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone hypersecretion' 
(SIADH) and is charcterised by excessive secretion of ADH resulting in hyponatremia and fluid overload (ADH basically dilutes the 
blood). 
 
SIADH has many causes, just remember that both antidepressants and antipsychotics can cause it. 
 
Risk factors for SIADH include:- 
 Being elderly 
 Being female 
 Being a smoker 
 Having medical co-morbidity 
 Polypharmacy 
 Low body weight 
 Low baseline sodium concentration 
 Reduced renal function 
 Warm weather 
SIADH normally develops within a few weeks of starting the new drug. 
 
Treatment usually consists of fluid restriction. In some cases demeclocycline is used.

questions.question_text: Pathological crying is also known as which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Pathological crying 
Pathological crying or laughing (aka 'pseudobulbar affect') is a condition characterised by sudden outbursts of crying in response to 
very minor stimuli without associated changes in mood. 
 
It has the following features: 
 Frequent, sudden loss of emotional control i.e. laughing or crying or both patient. 
 Occurrence in response to non-specific often inconsequential Stimuli (patient may laugh in response to sad news or cry in 
response to neutral stimuli like moving objects). 
 Lack of clear association with prevailing mood state. 
 
It can result from a number of different neurological conditions. It is often associated with strokes, one study found the frequency to 
be 11% a year after a stroke. 
 
When asked to select the treatment for pathological crying post-stroke, citalopram is generally the correct answer on the college 
questions most likely due to the original article in the Lancet where it out performed tricyclic antidepressants. However the evidence 
suggests that tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline and nortriptyline, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) 
such as sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine, and citalopram are effective in treating pathological crying a stroke.

questions.question_text: In a patient being evaluated for neuropsychiatric disturbances, a CT scan shows atrophy of head of caudate nucleus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Caudate atrophy = Huntington's disease 
 
Atrophy of the caudate nucleus would suggest Huntigton's disease. Wilson and Fahr's disease might show dense lesions in the 
caudate rather than atrophy and Alzheimer's and Pick's would be suggested by cortical atrophy. 
Basal ganglia 
The basal ganglia are a group of subcortical structures. Its main function is the control of movement but it may also play a part in 
some cognitive processes. 
 
The components of the basal ganglia are as follows:- 
 Striatum (caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens) 
 Subthalamic nucleus 
 Globus pallidus 
 Substantia nigra (divided into pars compacta and pars reticulate) 
 
The putamen and globus pallidus are collectively referred to as the lenticular nucleus. 
 
The connections of the basal ganglia are complicated but put simply, the cortex projects to the striatum, the striatum to the internal 
segment of the globus pallidus, the internal segment of the globus pallidus to the thalamus and the thalamus back to the cortex, 
thus creating a loop. 
 
There are four main conditions to be aware of that result from problems with the basal ganglia:- 
 Huntington's chorea (caudate nucleus) 
 Wilson's disease (copper deposition in basal ganglia) 
 Parkinson's disease (substantia nigra) 
 Hemiballism (subthalamic nucleus)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered to be the most common precipitating factor in Diogenes syndrome
questions.explanation:
Diogenes syndrome 
 
Diogenes syndrome (DS) is a behavioural disorder described in the clinical literature in elderly individuals: the classical constellation 
of symptoms of this condition include extreme neglected physical state, social isolation, domestic squalor, and tendency to hoard 
excessively (syllogomania) 
 
The estimated annual incidence of DS is 0.5 per 1000 of the population aged 60 or over living at home. It tends to occur in the 
elderly although younger individuals have been described (<65). 
 
The loss of a close relative who was caring for the patient appears to be the most important precipitating factor, initiating the 
deterioration in self-care in one third of cases. 
 
The syndrome is not listed in current classifications of diseases such as DSM-V or ICD-10 (rather it is a feature of an illness not a 
specific disease). It is seen in conditions such as dementia, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and alcoholism (although 
as many as 50% of DS patients have no history of psychiatric illness).

Mania (Maudsley Guidelines) 
The following algorithm is recommended by the Maudsley Guidelines (10th Edition) for the treatment of mania/ hypomania. 
 
1) Stop antidepressants (if on one) 
 
2) If not already on an antimanic medication 
 Consider an antipsychotic, valproate (avoid in women of childbearing age), or lithium 
 If response is inadequate combine antipsychotic and valproate or lithium 
 
3) If already on an antimanic 
 If on antipsychotic add lithium or valproate 
 If on lithium add an antipsychotic 
 If on valproate add an antipsychotic 
 If on carbamazepine add an antipsychotic 
 
Note that in each case compliance should be checked and levels taken where appropriate. 
 
Also note that the Guidelines suggest that short term benzodiazepines should be considered in all cases.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the least reliable risk factor for Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation:
During the 1960s and 1970s, aluminum emerged as a possible suspect in causing Alzheimer's disease. This suspicion led to 
concerns about everyday exposure to aluminum through sources such as cooking pots, foil, beverage cans, antacids and 
antiperspirants. Since then, studies have failed to confirm any role for aluminum in causing Alzheimer's. Almost all scientists today 
focus on other areas of research, and few experts believe that everyday sources of aluminum pose any threat.

Suicide following self-harm 
Most patients who self-harm do not go on to commit suicide. This poses a big challenge for risk assessment. 
 
A study (Hawton 2015) published in 2015 looked at UK rates of suicide following self-harm cases that had presented to hospital. 
 
Overall, 0.5% of individuals died by suicide in the first year following self-harm, of which 0.82% were males and 0.27% females. 
1.6% died by suicide over the two year period following self-harm (more occured in year two). 
 
Interestingly, another study (Murphy 2012) found the rate to be higher in the elderly (those over 60) and produced a rate of 1.5 
suicides in the first 12 months. In this study, the only significant risk factor for suicide following self-harm was the use of a violent 
method in the index episode.

A 75 year old lady with Cushing's syndrome is admitted to hospital with very late onset schizophrenia. Her daughter tells you that she is very 'fragile' and has previously sustained multiple bone fractures from minor falls. Which of the following antipsychotics would be the most appropriate in this case until further investigations are performed?
questions.explanation:
Cushing's disease results in excess glucocorticoid secretion by the adrenal glands and so osteoporosis. Olanzapine would 
therefore be the best initial option in this case until a DEXA scan could be done to either confirm or refute osteoporosis. 
Antipsychotics (hyperprolactinaemia) 
Hyperprolactinemia is associated with the use of antipsychotics (and very occasionally antidepressants). Dopamine inhibits 
prolactin and so dopamine antagonists increase prolactin levels. 
 
All antipsychotics cause measurable changes in prolactin but some do not increase levels beyond the normal range. The degree of 
prolactin elevation is dose related. 
 
It is often asymptomatic but is associated with the following:- 
 Galactorrhoea and breast growth 
 Amenorrhoea 
 Gynaecomastia 
 Hypogondism 
 Sexual dysfunction 
 
Psychiatric patients with long standing hyperprolactinaemia have an increased risk of:- 
 Osteoporosis 
 Breast cancer (females only) 
 
Antipsychotics known to cause significant hyperprolactinaemia include:- 
 All the typical antipsychotics 
 Risperidone 
 Amisulpride 
 Zotepine 
 
Drugs not usually associated with hyperprolactinaemia include:- 
 Clozapine 
 Aripiprazole 
 Quetiapine 
 Olanzapine 
 Ziprasidone 
 
Monitoring 
 
All patients should have a their prolactin measured before antipsychotic therapy and then should be asked about symptoms at three 
months (and if symptoms present it should be measured again). In cases where there are no symptoms, annual testing is 
recommended. 
 
Antipsychotics that increase prolactin should be avoided in the following (where possible): 
 Patients under 25 (before peak bone mass) 
 Patients with osteoporosis 
 Patients with a history of hormone dependent cancer 
 
Testing 
 
Samples should be taken at least 1 hour after eating or waking. Care must be taken to avoid stress during the proceedure as this 
can elevate prolactin. 
 
Gender Normal range 
Male 0-25 ng/ml (0-530 mlU/L) 
Women 0-20ng/ml (0-424 mlU/L) 
 
Treatment 
 
In symptomatic cases or where there is concern about long-term risk (the actual prolactin level is not really a big deal) the options 
are: 
 Switch to an alternative antipsychotic less prone to hyperprolactineamia 
 Alternatively, aripiprazole (at 3-6 mg/day) can be added in as this can lower prolactin levels (note that this is a small dose 
as the minimally effective daily dose is 10 mg). 
 The last option is to add a dopamine agonist such as amantadine or bromocriptine (but these have the potential to worsen 
psychosis). 
 
Maudsley Guidelines 11th Edition.

Mechanism of action 
It is important to know the mechanisms of action of the different drugs. These are common questions in the exam, and easy marks 
if you make an effort to learn them. 
 
Antidepressant Mechanism 
Mirtazapine Noradrenaline and serotonin specific antidepressant (NaSSa) 
5HT2 antagonist, 5HT3 antagonist, H1 antagonist, alpha 1 and alpha 2 antagonist, moderate muscarinic antagonist 
Venlafaxine Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) 
Duloxetine Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) also weak inhibitor of dopamine reuptake 
Reboxetine Noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (NaRI) 
St John's Wort Weak MAOI and weak SNRI (also considered by some to be a weak SSRI) 
Trazodone Weak antagonist and SARI (Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor)

Agomelatine Melatonergic agonist (MT1 and MT2 receptors) and 5-HT2C antagonist 
Bupropion (Zyban) Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI), and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist 
 
Antidementia drug Mechanism 
Donepezil Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor 
Antidementia drug Mechanism 
Rivastigmine Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and butyrylcholinesterase inhibitor 
Galantamine Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and binds allosterically to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor

Gabapentin GABA agonist

Phenytoin Stabilises Na channels

Amisulpride D2/D3 selective antagonist (low affinity selective antagonist of 'D2 like' receptors (D2=D3>D4) it has little affinity for D1
